1. Executive Summary & System Architecture

Deploying keyword spotting on edge microcontrollers requires strict balance across serial transport bandwidth, internal SRAM ceilings, numerical feature parity, and persistent storage. In this project, Team 1 (Paradise) designed, implemented, and validated an end-to-end audio pipeline on the ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 N16R8.

The system receives 144 one-second spoken commands across 6 classes (on, off, stop, go, _unknown, _silence), validates packet delivery using CRC-32 frames, stores audio in 8 MB OPI PSRAM, commits a 4.608 MB persistent image to LittleFS flash surviving power cuts, computes 40-band HTK log-mel features in real time using an optimized radix-2 FFT (683.75 μs/frame, 2,725× speedup), and sends features back to Python for dataset building and Nearest-Centroid keyword classification.

End-to-End Pipeline

team_audio.py (48 kHz Float32) → audio_codec.py (16 kHz Int16 S=1.0) → 0xA5 0x5A CRC-32 Framing → COM11 (Native USB CDC) / COM12 (UART 921.6k) → doorbell_board.ino (32 KB Ring Buffer, LittleFS /rec.bin) → features.h (Radix-2 FFT, 40 HTK Mels) → 0xB5 0x5B 'F' Frame Downlink → 7,056-Frame Clean Dataset → Nearest-Centroid Classifier (75.00% Accuracy) → 10-Page React Dashboard.

2. Mission 1: The Pipe (Data Rate & Data Type)

1. Aim
Measure throughput and packet framing overhead across UART (COM12) and native USB CDC (COM11), determine wire bandwidth limits for f32, i16, and i8, and evaluate real-time feasibility.
2. Background
UART transmits asynchronously with 1 start bit, 8 data bits, and 1 stop bit (10 bits/byte). Its theoretical throughput is baud / 10 bytes/second. Native USB CDC is packetized Full-Speed USB (12 Mbps line rate) handled by the ESP32-S3 internal USB PHY; baud rate is ignored, but transfer speed is limited by host-side USB scheduling and the board's RX ring buffer.
3. Prediction
Calculated before measuring:
  • 16 kHz f32 = 64,000 B/s (64,650 B/s with framing); i16 = 32,000 B/s (32,650 B/s); i8 = 16,000 B/s (16,650 B/s).
  • 115,200 baud UART maxes out at 11,520 B/s → cannot carry 16 kHz audio in real time.
  • 921,600 baud UART maxes out at 92,160 B/s → can carry 16 kHz f32, i16, and i8.
  • Native USB CDC will achieve >300 KB/s, independent of configured baud rate.
4. Method
Stream audio using student1_esp32/benchmarks/mission1_pipe_benchmark.py with feat=False, store="none". Measure speed at speed=0 across 115,200, 921,600, and 2,000,000 baud on COM12 and COM11. Test packet sizes: 8, 64, 320, 1024 samples/packet. Record board-measured time (ms) vs host send_seconds.
5. Observations
Port Baud Laptop Rate Board Rate Bad CRC Gaps Real-Time 16k i16
COM (COM12) 115,200 11,360.5 B/s 11,376.4 B/s 0 0 FAIL (2,809 ms)
COM (COM12) 921,600 90,726.0 B/s 90,909.2 B/s 0 0 PASS (987 ms)
COM (COM12) 2,000,000 194,535.1 B/s 194,726.9 B/s 0 0 PASS (982 ms)
USB (COM11) 115,200 501,455.3 B/s 332,181.9 B/s 13.0 0 PASS (982 ms, 0 err)
USB (COM11) 921,600 508,498.1 B/s 334,509.0 B/s 13.7 0 PASS (982 ms, 0 err)
6. Analysis
COM port rates strictly adhere to 10-bit UART physical limits (11.4, 90.9, 194.7 kB/s). USB CDC ignores baud entirely, achieving ~334 kB/s on board. At speed=0, unthrottled 64 KB bursts overflow the 32 KB RX buffer on USB. However, at speed=1.0, USB CDC and COM (≥921.6k) sustain zero packet drops and zero CRC errors. Small packet sizes (spp=8) incur 44.8% header overhead (26 KB headers on 32 KB data), whereas spp=320 incurs only 2.0% overhead.
7. What We Learnt
pyserial.write() returns when bytes enter local OS/USB drivers, not when the ESP32 receives them. Reliable benchmarking requires board-measured time (ms). Packet size must be ≥320 samples to avoid excessive frame header overhead.
8. LLM Log
Prompt: "How many bytes per second can you send to an ESP32-S3 over USB?"
LLM Response Summary: Full-Speed USB 1.1 achieves theoretical 12 Mbps (1.5 MB/s); practical bulk CDC yields 500–900 KB/s, independent of baud rate. UART bridge requires 10 bits/byte (baud / 10). Host OS buffering may cause write() to return before physical transmission.

3. Mission 2: What to Send & Where to Keep It

1. Aim
Implement audio quantization and packing in NumPy, quantify aliasing and Signal-to-Quantization-Noise Ratio (SQNR), configure 8 MB OPI PSRAM, and implement LittleFS flash persistence surviving power loss.
2. Background
The Nyquist-Shannon theorem requires pre-sampling low-pass filtering. Frequencies above fs/2 fold back into the baseband at |k*fs - f|. Int16 quantization provides ~98 dB theoretical SQNR, while int8 yields ~48 dB. ESP32-S3 internal SRAM is fragmented; buffering 144 seconds requires external PSRAM, and power-cut persistence requires LittleFS non-volatile flash storage.
3. Prediction
Team 1's room tone at 7,348.0 Hz will alias at 8 kHz to |8000 - 7348.0| = 652.0 Hz if anti-aliasing is disabled. Int16 with S=1.0 will provide >70 dB SQNR with 0% clipping; int8 will suffer severe quantization noise (~25 dB SQNR). Internal SRAM will hold <5 seconds of audio; PSRAM and LittleFS will hold all 144 seconds (4.608 MB).
4. Method
Evaluate silence clip 120 at 48 kHz vs 8 kHz with and without antialias=True. Measure SQNR across 144 clips for i16 S=1.0, i8 S=1.0, and i8 S=0.25. Test SRAM allocation ceiling, enable OPI PSRAM, implement cmdSave() in doorbell_board.ino using LittleFS, stream 144 clips, power-cycle the board, and verify flash CRC.
5. Observations
  • Anti-Aliasing: Tone at 7,348 Hz (-31.97 dB) folds to 652 Hz (-31.94 dB) without filter. Enabling antialias=True suppresses the peak by 51.82 dB down to -83.76 dB.
  • SQNR: i16 S=1.0 delivers 74.21 dB mean SQNR (0.00% clipping). i8 S=1.0 gives 25.98 dB; i8 S=0.25 gives 16.25 dB with 1.69% speech clipping.
  • SRAM vs PSRAM: Internal SRAM capped at 142,070 B (4.44 s). OPI PSRAM unlocked 8,388,608 B, storing all 4,608,000 B with 0 errors.
  • Flash Persistence: SAVE wrote 4,608,000 B to /rec.bin in 10.56 s. After power disconnection and reconnect, dump("flash") returned bit-exact CRC 0x55c3d431 (PSRAM was wiped).
Figure 2.1: 8 kHz Anti-Aliasing Spectral Comparison (7,348 Hz tone suppressed by 51.82 dB).
6. Analysis
Anti-aliasing must occur prior to decimation because digital filtering cannot separate folded tones once sampled. Int16 S=1.0 preserves speech fidelity with negligible distortion. Stock Arduino settings assign only 1.44 MB to LittleFS; our custom partitions.csv allocates 6.88 MiB, leaving 35.8% headroom after storing 144 clips.
7. What We Learnt
PSRAM is volatile and loses all contents on power cut. LittleFS requires custom partition tables for 16 MB flash. During dump("flash"), HWCDC dropped bytes during flash SPI reads until we configured a 32 KB TX buffer and 256-byte chunk pacing in firmware.
8. LLM Log
Prompt: "Why does an ESP32-S3 fail with 'ERR no psram' even though the chip has 8 MB PSRAM?"
LLM Response Summary: ESP32-S3 N16R8 uses Octal (OPI) PSRAM. Default Arduino IDE board configuration sets PSRAM to "Disabled" or "QSPI". It must be explicitly set to "OPI PSRAM" in the Tools menu; otherwise psramFound() returns false and heap allocation fails.

4. Mission 3: Features on the Board (Log-Mel Extraction)

1. Aim
Implement the exact Section 5 log-mel recipe in NumPy, optimize ESP32-S3 feature extraction in features.h to run within the 20 ms frame budget, and prove numerical parity within ≤0.05 dB.
2. Background
Log-mel spectrograms emulate human auditory perception. The recipe requires: 1) Framing (win=480, hop=320), 2) Hann windowing, 3) 512-pt FFT power spectrum, 4) 40 triangular HTK mel filterbanks (20–8000 Hz), 5) Log scaling: 10*log10(max(p, 1e-10)). A naive Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) requires $O(N^2)$ complex multiplications, violating real-time deadlines.
3. Prediction
Textbook starter DFT calling cosf/sinf 246,720 times per frame will take ~1.5–2.0 seconds per frame (100× slower than real time). An in-place Cooley-Tukey radix-2 DIT FFT with precomputed twiddle factor tables and sparse mel boundaries will run in under 1,000 μs (<1 ms).
4. Method
Implement reference_logmel.py in NumPy. Replace starter dft() in features.h with an iterative bit-reversal radix-2 FFT using precomputed LUTs (twRe, twIm) and sparse mel filter spans [melStart[m], melEnd[m]). Stream 10 seconds of audio at speed=1.0 on COM11 and compare per-frame compute_us, lag_s, and max dB difference vs NumPy.
5. Observations
Implementation Expected Frames Received Frames Mean Compute Time Max Lag Max Diff vs NumPy
Starter dft() 499 16 (483 lost) 1,863,425 μs (1.86 s) 29.56 s 0.000126 dB
Optimized Radix-2 FFT 499 499 (0 lost) 683.71 μs (0.68 ms) 0.0147 s 0.000072 dB
MFCC-13 (10 ms hop) 998 998 (0 lost) 714.22 μs 0.0203 s 0.000092 dB
Figure 3.1: 40-Band Log-Mel Spectrograms of All 6 Classes Generated from ESP32-S3 Features.
6. Analysis
Optimization achieved a 2,725× speedup. At 683.71 μs per 20 ms hop, the ESP32-S3 CPU duty cycle is only 3.42%, leaving a 29.2× compute margin. Max numerical error vs NumPy is 0.000072 dB (well within 0.05 dB limit). In a speed sweep (2× to 10×), feat=True and feat=False fail at the identical speed (8×, 256 KB/s), proving that serial ingress buffering—not compute—is the bottleneck.
7. What We Learnt
Trigonometric function calls (cosf/sinf) in loops are disastrous on microcontrollers. Precomputing twiddle factors and restricting filterbank multiply-accumulate operations to non-zero bins transforms an unusable pipeline into a production-grade DSP engine.
8. LLM Log
Prompt: "How long does a 512-point FFT take on an ESP32-S3 at 240 MHz?"
LLM Response Summary: A standard radix-2 DIT FFT implementation in C with look-up tables takes approximately 300 to 800 μs on an Xtensa LX7 core at 240 MHz. Using Espressif ESP-DSP SIMD assembly can push latency below 200 μs.

5. Mission 4: Nothing Lost (Loss Accounting & Labelled Dataset)

1. Aim
Prove complete transmission integrity over all 144 clips, recover sample alignment under packet loss injection (skip), generate a clean labelled feature dataset, and author the official Data Card.
2. Background
If a serial packet drops, naive sample counting causes subsequent audio frames to misalign in time, contaminating all downstream training labels. Packet loss must be detected via sequence numbers, and lost time must be zero-filled in firmware to preserve sample timestamps (first_sample). Frames straddling clip boundaries must be identified and handled.
3. Prediction
For 144 one-second clips at 16 kHz: 144 s × 16,000 = 2,304,000 samples. At 320 samples/packet: exactly 7,200 data packets. Feature frames per 1-s clip: 1 + (16000 - 480) // 320 = 49 frames; 144 clips × 49 = 7,056 clean frames. Continuous streaming across boundaries yields 7,199 total frames (143 straddling frames).
4. Method
Stream all 144 clips at speed=1.0 on COM11. Log packets_sent, frames_ok, seq_gaps, bad_crc, and samples. Run controlled loss test with skip=(10, 11, 200). Implement zero-fill gap recovery in doorbell_board.ino. Filter out 143 straddling boundary frames and export doorbell_team1_esp32_features.npz and .csv.
5. Observations
  • Full 144-Clip Run: 7,200 packets sent; frames_ok = 7,201 (7,200 data + 1 END); bad_crc = 0; seq_gaps = 0; samples = 2,304,000. Expected features: 7,199; received: 7,199 (0 lost).
  • Loss Accounting with skip=(10, 11, 200): Telemetry caught exactly 2 sequence gap events (gap of 2 packets at seq 10; gap of 1 packet at seq 200). Post-gap tail sample landed at 159,360 (exact expected alignment, 0 drift) vs 158,400 (-960 samples drift) prior to firmware fix.
  • Dataset Balance: Exactly 1,176 frames per class across all 6 classes (7,056 total clean frames).
Figure 4.1: Controlled Packet Drop Recovery (first_sample perfectly realigned to 159,360 with zero drift).
6. Analysis
Sequence numbers detect missing packets; CRC-32 detects corrupted bytes. In firmware, when a sequence jump occurs, inserting gap_pkts * samples_per_packet zeros into storeBuf, advancing st.samples, resetting fcount = 0, and skipping to the next hop boundary completely prevents timeline slippage. Excluding the 143 inter-clip frames prevents cross-label contamination during model training.
7. What We Learnt
Handling sequence gaps at packet 0 requires special care because seq=0 can drop on link connect. The firmware must check whether the first arriving packet has seq > 0 and insert initial zero padding accordingly.
8. LLM Log
Prompt: "How do you maintain audio feature frame alignment when UDP or serial packets are lost?"
LLM Response Summary: In streaming DSP, missing audio packets cannot simply be skipped; dropping samples causes all future FFT windows to slip in time. The receiver must synthesize silence (zero-padding) for the exact duration of the lost samples to maintain wall-clock phase and frame indexing.

6. Mission 5: Laptop vs. Board (Domain Shift & Classifier)

1. Aim
Quantify numerical domain shift between laptop float32 and ESP32 board features across formats (16k i16, 16k i8, 8k no-AA), train a Nearest-Centroid keyword spotter, and defend the shipping configuration.
2. Background
Fixed-point quantization, clipping, and aliasing alter feature distributions relative to Python float32 training data. A Nearest-Centroid classifier computes class centroids on standardized training features (80-dim: per-clip mean and std of 40 bands) and assigns test clips to the nearest centroid by Euclidean distance. Train/test splits must be stratified at the clip level (96 train / 48 test) to prevent data leakage.
3. Prediction
16 kHz int16 S=1.0 will exhibit negligible MAE (<0.01 dB) and produce identical classifier accuracy to laptop float32. Int8 will exhibit higher MAE (~1.0 dB) with slight accuracy degradation. 8 kHz without anti-aliasing will exhibit massive MAE (>5 dB) due to 7,348 Hz whine aliasing and will severely degrade classification.
4. Method
Compare all 4 hardware 144-clip feature runs against Python float32 reference using compare_features.py (MAE, RMSE, MaxAbs per band and class). Train Nearest-Centroid classifier on two-thirds of clips (96 clips) and evaluate on the remaining 48 clips using nearest_centroid_eval.py across all settings.
5. Observations
Audio & Feature Configuration MAE vs Float32 Ref Max Error Accuracy Macro F1
Laptop Float32 (16 kHz AA=True) 0.000000 dB 0.000 dB 75.00% 0.7356
ESP32 16 kHz i16 S=1.0 (Shipping) 0.003914 dB 0.124 dB 75.00% 0.7356
ESP32 16 kHz i8 S=1.0 1.089735 dB 16.426 dB 68.75% 0.6532
ESP32 16 kHz i8 S=0.25 0.821018 dB 34.247 dB 66.67% 0.6289
ESP32 8 kHz i16 (No-AA vs 8k AA Ref) 8.050974 dB 53.594 dB 25.00% 0.1642
Figure 5.1: Error Difference Heatmaps (16k i16 has virtually 0 error; 8k no-AA has massive bands 12–14 errors).
Figure 5.2: Confusion Matrices (Laptop Float32 and ESP32 16k i16 are 100% identical).
6. Analysis
ESP32 16 kHz i16 S=1.0 achieves bit-exact classification parity (75.00% accuracy) with the laptop float32 pipeline; their confusion matrices are identical. In contrast, 8 kHz without anti-aliasing causes bands 12–14 to suffer 20–31 dB MAE, collapsing classifier accuracy to 25.00% (random chance on 6 classes is 16.7%). Int8 S=0.25 clips speech peaks (34.2 dB max error), degrading accuracy to 66.67%.
7. What We Learnt
Minor quantization noise (0.004 dB) is completely benign for keyword spotting because it affects only silent bins below the speech signal floor. In contrast, aliasing injects artificial energy directly into high-frequency speech formants, catastrophic for machine learning.
8. LLM Log
Prompt: "Why does audio aliasing destroy speech recognition accuracy more than uniform quantization noise?"
LLM Response Summary: Uniform quantization noise behaves like white noise, uniformly distributed across all frequency bands. Aliasing, however, creates spurious tonal peaks reflected into lower frequencies that mimic or corrupt acoustic formants, misleading classifier weight vectors.

7. Official Data Card & Commitment Memo Summary

Official Data Card: Team 1 ("Paradise") Log-Mel Corpus

  • Source: 144 deterministic clips generated by team_audio.py (team=1) using speech_pool.npz (780 multi-voice recordings) mixed with Team 1 simulated room acoustics (7,347.98 Hz whine, 100 Hz hum, Gaussian noise).
  • Acquisition Hardware: Physical ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 N16R8 on COM11 (Native USB CDC).
  • Audio Configuration: 16,000 Hz, mono, int16 <i2, scale S=1.0, antialias=True.
  • Feature Dimensions: 40 HTK mel bands, win=480, hop=320, 512-pt FFT, float32.
  • Dataset Volume & Balance: 7,056 clean frames (1,176 frames per class across on, off, stop, go, _unknown, _silence). Exactly 49 frames per 1-second clip.
  • Straddling Frames Policy: 143 inter-clip frames (spanning 320 samples of clip $c$ and 160 samples of clip $c+1$) were discarded to eliminate label leakage.
  • Loss & Integrity: 0 packets lost, 0 bad CRCs, 0 duplicates, bit-exact CRC-32 (0x55c3d431) verified across power cuts.
  • Out-of-Scope Uses: Cannot be used to claim far-field, reverberant outdoor doorbell accuracy; train/test splits must split by clip_id, never by frame.

9. Bug Tracker, Limitations & Conclusion

Resolved Engineering Bugs (Stage A & Stage B Audit Trail)

Bug ID Severity Root Cause Engineering Resolution
SA-01 Critical HWCDC dropped TX bytes during flash reads in dump("flash"). Added Serial.setTxBufferSize(32768) and 256-B paced chunks in writeAll().
SA-02 Critical Packet loss caused post-gap audio sample timeline to slip in time. Firmware synthesizes zero padding, increments st.samples, resets fcount=0.
SA-03 High Starter DFT took 1,863 ms per frame, dropping 96.8% of frames. Rewrote with radix-2 DIT FFT + twiddle LUT + sparse mel bounds (684 μs, 2,725× speedup).
BUG-01 High Student 4 compared 8k No-AA against 8k No-AA instead of filtered 8k Ref. Re-ran comparisons with speech_pool.npz against true 8 kHz antialias=True.
BUG-02 Medium Frontend Comparison view displayed outdated fallback text. Updated ComparisonPage.tsx and MlEvaluationPage.tsx copy and descriptions.
BUG-03 Medium Shared contract v1.0.0 lacked documentation for Vite /repo/* bridge. Incremented frontend_api_contract.json to v1.1.0 documenting all bridges and plots.
BUG-04 Low Python MockBoard did not synthesize zero fill when seq=0 dropped. Updated serial_sender.py to handle drop_seq_0 with exact sample padding.

Project Limitations & Future Work

  1. Synthesized Audio Stream: Audio originates from synthetic Python playback over USB serial rather than a live physical I2S MEMS microphone (e.g. INMP441) in an acoustically reverberant room.
  2. Dataset Volume: 144 one-second clips (48 test clips) with mean+std pooling restricts keyword separability between phonetically similar commands (e.g., on vs go).
  3. USB Burst Limitation: Native USB CDC drops packets during unthrottled bursts ≥ 256 KB/s due to the 32 KB hardware FIFO. DMA double-buffering is recommended for higher speed.
  4. On-Device Inference: Future revisions will embed a quantized INT8 1D-CNN directly on the ESP32-S3 using ESP-NN SIMD vector instructions, eliminating feature streaming entirely.

Conclusion

Team 1 (Paradise) has delivered a robust, reproducible, and fully integrated Smart Doorbell Edge AI system. Physical testing on the ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 N16R8 confirms 0 lost packets, sub-millisecond feature extraction, 100% bit-exact flash persistence across power cycles, identical keyword spotting accuracy to host Python, and comprehensive full-stack visualization. The project is fully verified and ready for final submission.
